lesson.title: Why n - 1? Understanding Degrees of Freedom
lesson.summary: Degrees of freedom count how many values in a sample are free to vary once certain quantities, like the sample mean, are fixed, and this number determines the exact shape of the t-distribution used in later procedures.
lesson.body:
Whenever a statistic is calculated from a sample, some of the information in that sample gets used up in the process. Degrees of freedom count how much information is left over, specifically, how many values in the sample are still free to vary once other quantities computed from that same sample are held fixed. For a single sample of size n used to estimate a population mean, the relevant degrees of freedom is n - 1.

Here is why. Once you know the sample mean, xbar, of a sample of five values, and you know four of the five individual deviations from that mean, the fifth deviation is no longer free to be anything: it is forced to take on whatever value makes all five deviations sum to exactly zero, since deviations from the mean always sum to zero by definition. Only 4 of the 5 deviations are free, the last one is determined by the rest. In general, for a sample of size n, only n - 1 of the deviations from the sample mean can vary independently, the last is always fixed by the requirement that they sum to zero. That is where the n - 1 in degrees of freedom comes from.

Degrees of freedom matters because the sample standard deviation, s, which is calculated using those n - 1 free deviations, is used later as an estimate of the unknown population standard deviation sigma. Using s instead of the true sigma introduces extra uncertainty, and the amount of that extra uncertainty depends on how many degrees of freedom went into estimating s. A sample with only a few degrees of freedom gives a shakier estimate of variability than a sample with many. This single number, df = n - 1 for a one-sample situation, turns out to determine the exact shape of the probability distribution used in the procedures that follow, the t-distribution, which is the subject of the next section.
